analysis.one_liner: Bars states from adopting clean-air rules that limit the sale of new gasoline-powered vehicles.
analysis.headline: The bill to block state rules limiting gasoline-car sales has sat without action in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since its referral in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Clean Air Act, states like California can adopt stricter vehicle emission rules than the federal government, but only if the EPA grants them a waiver. California has used that authority to require a rising share of new cars sold in the state to be zero-emission, and other states follow its rules. This bill would change the law so that no state can get such a waiver for any rule that directly or indirectly limits the sale of gasoline-powered cars, and would require the EPA to take back waivers already granted going back to January 2022. In effect, it would stop states from phasing out new gas-car sales.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and sellers of gasoline-powered vehicles and the oil and gas industry gain the most, because state rules that would shrink their market for new combustion-engine cars are blocked. Buyers who prefer or depend on gasoline vehicles, including lower-income drivers and people without home charging, keep the full range of combustion models on dealer lots.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies, gas-car sellers, and some car buyers

how_it_helps.text: It amends the Clean Air Act so that no state can get or keep an EPA waiver for standards that directly or indirectly limit the sale or use of new internal-combustion-engine vehicles.

It requires the EPA to revoke any waiver granted between January 1, 2022 and enactment if the state standards limit gasoline-vehicle sales, and bars the EPA from bringing amended state standards under existing waivers.

analysis.who_pays: States lose the power to set their own tailpipe rules; residents bear more vehicle air pollution for longer. Automakers and suppliers that invested in EV production lines to meet state mandates face weaker, less certain demand for those products.
analysis.who_pays_short: States and residents breathing more pollution

drawbacks.text: It revokes Clean Air Act waivers that were already granted, including California's authority to require a shift to zero-emission vehicles, reaching back to rules granted as early as January 1, 2022.

It permanently bars any state, including California and the states that follow its rules, from setting emission standards that limit the sale of gasoline-powered vehicles, removing the strongest state-level lever for cutting vehicle pollution.

Supporters would respond that this protects consumers in states whose dealers would otherwise be required to sell a quota of electric vehicles regardless of local demand, and keeps the pace of the EV transition in federal rather than state hands.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest argument for the bill is that it keeps the decision about how fast to shift away from gasoline cars at the federal and consumer level rather than mandating it state by state, which supporters say protects buyers who cannot afford an EV or lack a place to charge one. The cost is that it strips states of the authority they have used since 1967 to set stronger clean-air rules than the federal government, rewrites the rules retroactively to cancel waivers already granted, and would slow the transition to electric vehicles that most auto companies had already begun, with consequences for air quality and climate. The retroactive revocation of existing waivers is the hardest provision for a good-faith opponent to accept: it does not just stop future state rules, it reaches back and voids rules states are already operating under.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no movement since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 13, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Since that referral, no further action has been listed in the bill's record: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.
It carries seven Republican cosponsors and no Democratic cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost; the bill has simply gone nowhere in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill has gone nowhere

for.name: Rep. John Joyce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar state clean-air waivers that limit gasoline-vehicle sales.

for.name: 7 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all seven cosponsors are Republicans.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all seven cosponsors are Republicans, and no Democrat has signed on, but no vote has been taken so the partisan split has not been tested.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Blocking state EV mandates preserves long-term gasoline and diesel demand that state zero-emission-vehicle rules would have eroded. The bill protects the market their core product depends on.
Dealers are spared state quotas requiring them to stock and sell electric vehicles in set proportions. Dealerships that are unprepared for EV sales benefit most.

Makers of gasoline vehicles keep a guaranteed market for internal-combustion models, while companies that had invested heavily in meeting zero-emission-vehicle targets face weaker demand for those plans. Most large automakers had already built EV strategies around the state rules.

industries.industry: Electric vehicle makers and charging companies
industries.note: State mandates were a major policy driver of EV demand and charging infrastructure. Removing them slows that buildout and the companies that depend on it.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has had no action since its committee referral, and standalone bills of this kind rarely move on their own. The underlying goal has, however, already been achieved by other means: in 2025, Congress passed and the President signed resolutions revoking federal approval of California's electric-vehicle mandate under the Congressional Review Act, which is widely reported. That makes this bill largely redundant, and its most likely path is to remain dormant in committee unless attached to a larger vehicle.
